Question: An ordinary clock in a factory is running slow so that the minute hand passes the hour hand at the usual dial positions (\(12\) o’clock, etc.) but only every \(69\) minutes. At time and one-half for overtime, the extra pay to which a \(\$4.00\)-per-hour worker should be entitled after working a normal \(8\)-hour day by that slow-running clock is:
Solution:
The minute hand passes the hour hand whenever it gains one complete turn on it. On an accurate ordinary clock, their speeds are \(1/60\) and \(1/720\) turn per minute, so the minute hand gains
\[
\frac1{60}-\frac1{720}=\frac{11}{720}
\]
turn per minute. Consecutive passings therefore occur every \(720/11\) minutes of displayed clock time.

The slow clock takes \(69\) real minutes to traverse that same interval. Since it retains the usual hand positions and gearing, the ratio of real elapsed time to displayed elapsed time is
\[
\frac{69}{720/11}=\frac{253}{240}.
\]
Eight displayed hours are \(480\) displayed minutes, so the worker actually works
\[
480\cdot\frac{253}{240}=506
\]
minutes. The overtime beyond a normal eight real hours is \(506-480=26\) minutes.

Time and one-half makes the overtime rate \(\tfrac32\cdot\$4=\$6\) per hour. Hence the extra pay beyond the normal day's wages is
\[
\$6\cdot\frac{26}{60}=\boxed{\$2.60},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
